user_history.review_text:
This is a snare drum that flies under the radar because you don't hear much about it if you frequent the various drum forums on the web. However, it's a bargain and one of the better snare drums on the market at any price point.

The main characteristic is projection. This snare drum can be loud. The Yamaha style wood hoops attenuate ringing and over- and undertones, but there is still a fair amount of resonance available if you tune it open.

Since the hoops are the unique feature I'll focus on those. They are based on what is commonly called the "Yamaha" hoop. The ones on this drum are made by PDP and sold separately as [[ASIN:B005DTWCZE Pacific Drums 14", 10 Lug Wood Hoops]]. If your playing entails a lot of cross sticking or heavy backbeats you will love them. They do entail a major trade-off and that is the loss of sensitivity as you play closer to the edge. For many style of music that level of nuance isn't required.

Construction is first rate. The shells are 10-ply, which accounts for why these project so well. The edges are a relatively sharp 45 degree cut that I would normally round over, but work perfectly with the heavier hoops. The hardware is heavily plated and rock solid. I love the Gladstone-style throw-off. It is smooth and engages and disengages totally as opposed to some throw-offs that still leave a little contact between the snare wire plates and the head.

Overall this is a wonderful snare drum that has surprising tone and a lot of features for a small price tag. You literally could not purchase the parts and build one for less.
user_history.review_title: A best kept secret

features: Pair of retractable wire jazz brushes with durable high-impact plastic handles.
description: The brushes have infinitely adjustable brush spreads capable of maintaining any playing position. A 6" spread and extra heavy gauge wire provide maximum coverage and sound. The oversized triangular metal pull rod doubles as an excellent beater for cymbal work.

user_history.review_text:
This is the heaviest and loudest pair of brushes I have ever used. Frankly these are not for jazz, but there appears to be a resurgence of interest in brush playing that may have been sparked by Florian Alexandru-Zorn's excellent book/DVD package titled [[ASIN:3933136849 The Complete Guide to Playing Brushes: Brush Skills for Playing Jazz and Pop Music (Book & DVD)]].

What makes this such a hefty brush is the .575 inch diameter handle and wide 5 inch bristle spread. The bristles are heavy gauge - even heavier than the [[ASIN:B004SX78T6 Vic Firth Russ Miller Signature Brush]] - and projects more than any brush I have ever played.

Frankly I am not wild about the feel or balance, but I am used to much lighter and thinner brushes. If you play heavier sticks you will probably welcome these if more mainstream brush models felt like toys in your hands. Personal preferences about weight and diameter aside, I am also not very fond of the handles, which I felt were slippery when my hands sweat. I will give a big plus to the pull rods that allow you to smoothly adjust the fan to just about any width and they will stay in place without slipping in or out.

If you are a rock or other music style drummer who is exploring brushes and normally play heavier music (with heavy sticks), these may be ideal. If you play mostly light amplified or acoustic music and your preferred stick is a 7A you may want to leave these alone and check out more traditional size brushes.
user_history.review_title: Heavy and loud

user_history.review_text:
I was warned against this brand (and Behringer and Pyle-Pro) when I was shopping for a small PA system. I was so taken with the features and price of this model that I made the purchase and for two years was pleased. Then it fried as predicted by those who advised me.

When it was working this mixed put out what I considered to be very good sound, I did not use the effects much, but did play around with them and was impressed. The mixer was for a home practice space, so it did not get lugged around to gigs, and it also spent its entire life in a smoke-free, climate controlled environment.

When it died, which was abruptly, everything including the power light shut down. The first frustration was locating the fuse, which I finally did with the help of the manual (which is pretty good.) Getting to it required removing the outer case, which proved to be nearly impossible because after I removed all of the screws on the back and sides, the case would not budge. Next, I took it to a local repair ship, which enjoys a good reputation. When the technician saw the brand he sort of frowned - a foreshadowing of what followed. He determined that the problem was the power supply. The first hiccup was the length of time it took to get a replacement from Phonic - 6 weeks. Next, as soon as the new one was installed and the mixer powered up it fried the second power supply. I already had $120 invested into repairs, so instead of throwing good money after bad I wrote it off and purchased a [[ASIN:B001Q5S99M Peavey XR8300 8 Channel 600 watt Powered Mixer]], which is what I should have done in the first place.

One can make the argument that I got my money's worth from this mixer since it lasted for two years, but that is not the point. First, it probably had less than 40 hours of actual use on it, and second, the brand does not seem to be held in high regard considering the warnings that I should have heeded before buying it. The episode during the failed repair cycle does not bode well for Phonic logistics either. Moral of this story is if you are shopping for a powered mixer, and especially one you want to depend on for live gigs, do not be blinded by an array of features and cut-rate price because you may discover as I did that you get what you pay for. Peavey, Yamaha and Mackie all have models with comparable features that, while more expensive, enjoy a solid reputation for reliability.
user_history.review_title: Nice fetures but not reliable

user_history.review_text:
If you routinely play Latin and Brazilian grooves with brushes check these out. While this model can also be used in more traditional forms of jazz, I have found that the feel of the larger brush area, as well as the nylon itself, is not optimum for ballads and some straight ahead playing. Of course, that may just be me set in my ways. In the hands of other drummers they may be perfect for those styles.

The brushes are remarkably well balanced considering that nearly half the length is comprised of the bristles. The handle is also relatively heavy, but I am guessing that the ball shape on the butt end is what gives these such a nice balance and feel.

One of the reasons why I mentioned that these are not optimum for ballads is the nylon does not make the traditional, legato sweeping sound that I use to mark quarter notes. On the other hand, for fast, staccato rhythms this brush is hard to beat.

This is also an ideal brush for Americana and roots music that uses cajons for percussion, so do not limit these to jazz. In fact, even if you play rock (and especially alternative rock) check out [[ASIN:3933136849 The Complete Guide to Playing Brushes: Brush Skills for Playing Jazz and Pop Music]] for some excellent tips and ideas.

target_product.review_text:
I purchased one of these because the passive model I also own - the [[ASIN:B000KUA8G6 BEHRINGER ULTRA-DI DI400P]] - doesn't always provide a transparent connection to some mixers (especially integrated mixers in some powered speakers.) Also, the output of my Roland KC-110 is not friendly to some mixers, and this solved that problem as well. So, compared to the DI400P this one has the features that will take care of those pesky instances. For my home studio I use the DI400P. When I am going to jams or showcase performances this is the DI that I bring.

Since every 'foreign' mixer I've used this with had phantom power I cannot state one way or the other how long batteries last. As an added measure or preparedness, though, I carry a spare battery and an [[ASIN:B00KAPGLQC InnoGear 1- Channel 48V Phantom Power Supply]], which I tested with this and it works perfectly. I prefer to NOT add complexity, but I have learned from experience that when things inevitably go wrong it's nice to have more than one fall back solution.

This is one of the most transparent DI boxes I have ever used. There is zero noise or coloring from either the output or the link (which is just a pass-through). That is one of my most used features because I can go directly to the mixer while simultaneously using the KC-110 or Mackie SRM150 as a monitor.

If you have control of your own equipment, up to and including a mixer, you may be able to get by with the less expensive DI400P. However, if you are connecting to host or house systems this is the DI to get. Mine has proven to be super reliable as well as functional.

user_history.review_text:
The BOSS RC-500 sets the new gold standard in looper pedals. Looping can get extremely complex, and no one pedal is likely to offer everything on a given player’s wish list in terms features, interface, and connectivity. But having used some less sophisticated loopers in the past, and heavily researched the current alternatives, I do feel that the RC-500 offers the most comprehensive solution to looping in a single unit. It would be impossible to cover everything the pedal does, so I will highlight the most notable pros and cons below.

PROS:
The primary selling point of the new BOSS looper lineup (which applies also to the compact RC-5 and drum pattern-oriented RC-10R) is the 32-bit sound engine. There’s a lot of debate online about how much a “32-bit” sound engine really matters. After all, “CD quality” is said to be 16-bit resolution with a 44.1 kHz sampling rate. But when it comes to capturing audio from a variety of instruments at different output levels (and then overdubbing that material with subsequent layers of audio), a poor sound engine will begin to show itself rather easily. This is where my former looper (the DigiTech Jamman Solo XT) started to fall short. Feature-wise, the Jamman was really quite useful, but I was constantly battling clipping when playing back loops. Essentially, if the audio was recorded at too high of a level, the playback would have crackles and static over it, which completely ruined the performance.

The RC-500’s sound engine – as far as I can tell – seems to be almost entirely free from this problem, and for this, I can forgive a lot of other shortcomings. I’m not an audio expert, but the best explanation I’ve been able to find is that the 32-bit engine has considerably higher headroom to avoid digital clipping. So the RC-500 sounds excellent, even while layering distorted guitars, synths, and other higher-output instruments. That’s a very big deal to me.

The RC-500 also features two tracks, which is a new feature for me. You can record these in parallel (played at the same time) or in parallel (one after the other), and it makes the RC-500 flexible to a lot of different creative approaches. Back from the RC-30 are the popular output sliders for quick live adjustments to levels of your two loops.

The (separate) rhythm track options and quantization of the drum tracks into perfect loop lengths is also a key feature for me. I believe there are 16 kits and several dozen rhythm patterns to choose from, and each of those has an “A” and “B” variation. Not only does it feel more like playing with other musicians, but it’s a more inspired way of keeping in time and practicing accurately versus playing with a simple metronome.

Finally, you get three footswitches on the device, plus the ability to assign 10 more (2 with a plug-in footswitch like the FS-6/7; 8 more with MIDI). Without this additional control a lot of the RC-500’s functionality would be trapped behind menus, and rarely used. There’s a few hitches to how MIDI is implemented, but I did like how basically EVERYTHING can be customized, even the buttons and knobs on the unit itself. I also really liked that the RC-500 is capable of running on 4 AA batteries – I’m getting about 3-4 hours of use on a set of Eneloop rechargeables. That’s a somewhat rare option to have given the digital nature of looping, and particularly on a unit this complex.

CONS:
I think the most important “drawback” to understand about the RC-500 is that it does not offer a “plug-and-play” experience, and may not be for everyone. While you have 3 footswitches and a somewhat clutter-free interface, there is a definite learning curve to setting up the RC-500 to work in a manner that works for you “on the fly”. The left footswitch handles the usual “REC/PLAY/UNDO” functionality, but from there it gets a little more complicated. The 2nd footswitch is a “STOP” button, which is great, but it only stops the current track, not the other track or the rhythm. Those features can be assigned via MIDI. Likewise, the 3rd switch flips between track control, or you can long-press it and the LED indicates purple, which means you can play or stop both tracks simultaneously. It’s a reasonable design choice, but like so many things on the RC-500, you might never figure it out without the manual or a tutorial video.

There are some annoyances with MIDI, also. BOSS does not include the 3.5mm-to-DIN MIDI cable you need to use with the device, and you have to use the certain kind that BOSS manufactures (about $18 for one), or it probably will not work. The MIDI assignments are saved PER PATCH, not universally. While this does allow you to set up different controls on different memory slots, it’s a massive pain to set up. The workaround is to create a “template” blank memory with the settings you want, and then copy that to all 99 slots.

I also need to mention that the RC-500 struggles with using its two tracks in “Verse -> Chorus” manner. In other words, you would assume that could record one part of a song as Track 1, and then set up a “chorus” or second part of the song as Track 2 and switch back and forth. You can do this, but not “out of the box” and not without some limitation as to the timing and duration of each track. It’s too much to get into here, but there are entire YouTube videos looking at workarounds for how to do this more effectively, which is disappointing.

Finally, while it should be evident to anyone looking at the device, the RC-500 is not “small”, nor is it terribly affordable. I have an HX Stomp modeler on my pedal board, and the RC-500 is essentially the same size – about the same as 2 or 3 compact effects pedals. It’s reasonable given the importance of looping to practice and performance, but if you don’t care about having two separate recording tracks, it might make more sense to look at something like the RC-5.

SUMMARY:
The RC-500 is not a “perfect” looper, but I highly doubt such a device exists or will ever exist. But what you need a looper to do above all else is to sound good and be durable enough to stand up to abuse. BOSS’ reputation is unmatched in both categories, and the RC-500 is no exception. The drum patterns are great, and although I’m not completely new to looping, doing it with the RC-500 feels like playing on another level. If you feel that you need the complexity and functionality it offers – or might in the future – it’s definitely one to consider.

user_history.review_text:
The Mooer Blues Crab, simply put, is a faithful clone of the fabled 90's-era Marshall Bluesbreaker pedal. That pedal was long ago discontinued, but has experienced a surge of interest in the past 15 years or so with pedals either cloning or "inspired by" the original Bluesbreaker. That list includes the King/Prince of Tone, JHS Morning Glory, Snouse Blackbox, and Wampler Panthon, among many others. I actually owned a v1 Snouse Blackbox, but sold it, and have been pleasantly surprised how close this Mooer Blues Crab reproduces that sound.

A few things note about the Blue Crab and this style of overdrive. First, this is very much a light-to-medium gain overdrive pedal that is valued for its transparency. Similar to how one would use a Klon, it's meant more to enhance the flavor of the rest of your signal chain, as opposed to completely taking it over. But I find that it excels with both clean and dirty amps. Into a fully-clean Fender Twin, it adds just a bit of "tube-like" grit while retaining that clean "sparkle" on the upper end.

Second, this is a clone - not a mod - of the original 1990's circuit...for better and worse. The original Bluesbreaker did not have a ton of output, and I find that the Blues Crab is at unity gain around 2:00 or 3:00 on the volume knob with most setting. But because it is meant as an "always on" overdrive, this is not really a problem, and you can stack it with additional drives afterwards if you are looking for more gain or output.

Finally, I want to say a word about Mooer. Yes, these are Chinese-made clones, often based on or copying popular circuits from years ago. But Mooer, in particular, was also hugely influential in the "micro pedal" trend of the last 10-15 years. I'm not even sure it's fully accurate to call a pedal a clone when they were among the first manufacturers to take pedals like Bluesbreakers, Tubescreamers, and OCD's, cramp them in to enclosures 1/3 or 1/2 the size of the original, and sell them at more affordable prices. Some of the Chinese budget pedals are made poorly, but the Mooers are solid, and the Blues Crab is one of their best efforts.

I bought the Vox Amplug AC30 and loved it so much, it probably doubled (or tripled) the amount of time I play guitar. I loved it so much I went out and got the more expensive (by $10) Joe Satriani Signature Amplug. I liked the Satriani model also because it covered a different tonal range than the AC30, and delay feature is a lot of fun. But I had serious questions about the Classic Rock Amplug. Why did have only a 4-star review on Amazon - among the lowest for any of the fabulous Amplug products. Would it be only a "one trick pony"?

Well, I have to tell you, I was completely blown away by how great the Classic Rock Amplug is, and I'm now even more blown away by some of these negative reviews. I've tried out a number of effects pedals for plugging into an actual guitar amplifier, and many pedal users are seeking what they call a "Marshall-in-a-box". In other words, they want a effects pedal that will single-handedly transform whatever amp they have into the sound of a miniaturized stack of Marshalls. Believe it or not, the Vox Classic Rock on higher gain settings is about as close to a "Marshall" sound as I can imagine. And it comes in a small, plastic headphone amplifier that runs on 2 AAA batteries and costs all of $39.99.

Functionally, the Classic Rock Amplug is the same as the AC30 - three dials for gain, tone, and volume, an aux in jack (for MP3 players), a headphone jack, and an on/off switch. But that's where the similarities end. While the excellent AC30 model simulates the boxy, sparkly sound of a tube amplifier, the Classic Rock packs some PUNCH. The low end presence on this thing (even through a $20 set of entry-level Sony headphones from Target) is significantly greater than on the AC30. More importantly, the sound doesn't deteriorate with higher volumes. There are plenty of ways you can try to play guitar through headphones, but most of them become a static-filled mess as soon as you turn up the volume. Amazingly, the tiny Amplug has plenty of power on tap, and the "overdrive" is controlled through analog circuitry, with amazing clarity.

But the real surprise in the Classic Rock Amplug (and the point upon which I disagree with several other reviewers here) are the clean and slightly overdrive tones as you roll back on the gain knob. Several reviewers referred to the clean tones as weak, or claimed that there were no clean tones. Yet, with both my Les Paul and a Strat, I was able to set the Volume at around 6-8 and the gain at about level 2 and get a very nice clean tone without loss of volume. If any dirt was remaining, a slight rollback on the guitar volume further cured the problem. Even better, playing a Strat into the Classic Rock with the gain set somewhere between 2 to 4 actually created a Tubescreamer-like blues tone! This tone was one of the audio demos offered on Vox's website, but I didn't believe it for myself until I plugged the Classic Rock in and dialed in that tone.

Long story short, the Classic Rock is extremely powerful, but more verstaile than I thought. It can do the high-gain Marshall tones I expected, but also offers a wide array of clean or slightly-overdriven tones. It might even be more versatile than the AC30 Amplug, though I remain pretty loyal to the AC30. The good news is that the two models are different enough and cheap enough that you can own both. Highly recommend the Classic Rock - 5 stars.

The Behringer UCG102 device is an aging (yet affordable) piece of hardware that offers the intriguing option of plugging your guitar directly into the USB port of a computer. This opens up a number of possibilities for recording or simply for playing with headphones. For the budget player, it could be argued that a mere $32 investment unlocks a world of free amp modeling and recording possibilities.

However, while the actual hardware is compact and seems function properly, there are some significant problems here. First and foremost, there is the problem of getting the device to work, getting the software to recognize it, and configuring it to run without significant "latency" (which is a delay effect where you don't hear a played note immediately when it's played, which can make monitoring anywhere from frustrating to impossible). The UCG102 runs on an ASIO driver. They include an older version with the software, and you can snoop around online and find other options. But that doesn't mean it will necessarily work with your software, or work well if it does. For example, Audacity is a popular "freeware" program you can use to record and mix audio files on the computer. I've been told that Audacity doesn't work with ASIO drivers, and when I got it to record, the latency issues rendered it unusable.

You do receive two other software options with the device. The first is energyXT2, which I believe includes a license for the compact version. In theory, this program should work like Audacity and contains a number of amp models and effects, in addition to drum and bass track loops. However, I have had little luck figuring out how to monitor and record with this program. I'm sure it CAN work, but if you need a computer science degree to figure it out, that's really not ideal for a budget product.

The second item is a trial disc with Guitar Combos by Native Instruments. So far, this has been the most impressive of the options offered. You can demo three different amp simulators (Vox, Fender, and Marshall) and then enter a code to unlock one of the three. I like that it gives you an interface similar to a real guitar amp, which allows you to dial in some realistic tones. It's also the only program I've been able to get the headphone jack to play through both ears in (there are problems with recognizing mono vs. stereo). I adjusted the sound quality to get latency down to 8 miliseconds, which is just into the range where I don't notice it as a problem. Still, while the models sound good, I'm not sure how often I would bother plugging into my computer just to do basic playing and recording.

Shortly after ordering this device, I discovered that my sound card has a blue "line in" audio jack on the back. By running a simple 1/8" to 1/4" audio cable from my pedal board to the sound card, I can do direct recording, which is monitored through my computer speakers (no latency) and sounds great. Even better, this method works through Audacity and allows me to record and layer tracks. If the UCG102 worked as advertised, it would be a more convenient way of doing this, but I simply can't recommend it for most people. I feel like there's "4-star" potential somewhere in this device, but I doubt I'll ever have the patience to unlock it. 3 stars.

I am going to post this review and revisit it as necessary, since I have had very up-and-down impressions of the new Headrush FRFR-108 since it first arrived. I’m landing on a 4-star rating because I’ve come to believe that some of my initial disappointment with the device - which was quite strong - was bit unfair given the unit’s compact size and budget pricing.

The FRFR-108 offers a new entry point for portability and affordability for guitar modelers, but it also isn’t those things. What I mean by that is that this is essentially a repurposed Alto TS308 PA speaker, except “branded” for guitar and without a dedicated microphone preamp. One look at the rear panel and you will instantly see similarities, from the location and style of the dual input XLR/TRS jacks to the volume knobs, switches, and “Made in China” designation. What the FRFR-108 offers is a “full range, flat response” speaker that, in theory, should be able to be used with everything from guitar modelers to bass guitar to synthesizers and drum machines.

In practice, however the FR-108 has a noticeable shortcoming in its clarity with clean, low frequency notes. Don’t get me wrong: the speaker has TONS of power. I purchased it to use with my HX Stomp guitar modeler, and I only had the thing turned up to “4”, and even that was probably louder than I needed for basement-level practicing. Across most of the frequencies where guitar lives, the FRFR-108 sounds great, and very accurately conveyed the preamp and cabinet modeling provided by the HX Stomp. The mids are cutting, the highs are jangly and articulate (provided you have the input device properly set up), and there is absolutely no shortage of low end volume particularly when using the FRFR-108 in “floor wedge” configuration.

But it didn't take long for me to notice that lower notes played on guitar, and particularly bass guitar and synths with lower frequencies, sounded fuzzy or distorted on the FRFR-108, even at pretty moderate volumes. At first, I suspected the culprit was a rattle or vibration, as it sounded more like something on the unit was resonating, but after removing the grill, the noise was unchanged.

Disappointing as this was, I came to remember that this is one of the smaller and more affordable FRFR options that can reasonably handle guitar, let alone trying to run bass or other devices with low frequencies through it. And while I doubt that the FRFR-112 or many of the 10" or 12" alternatives to this speaker suffer from this problem, those speakers also tend to be more expensive and can be quite a bit larger/heavier. At only 17 inches wide and just under 20 pounds in weight, the FRFR-108 puts out huge sound in a compact package (the FRFR-112, by comparison, weighs 35 pounds).

I also think the 8" speaker makes a lot of sense because of power/volume scaling. A 12" speaker isn't ALWAYS better than an 8" speaker, and if your goal is just to play out loud at lower volumes, the smaller speaker might actually convey a more balanced signal. I find that the FRFR-108 does this quite well.

I do not know if the Headrush FRFR-108 is a "forever" solution for me, and it's more of "rebrand" than an original design. But I do think this could be a useful companion to guitar modelers, and a lot of people simply don't need or want the additional volume or price that a larger unit involves. As long as your expectations of it remain realistic, it's a viable FRFR option for guitar and other audio sources.

target_product.review_text:
These picks really are special and are a crucial component of The Edge's patented "Vox chime", fed into a dual delay pedal with modulation, and then into the front end of a Vox AC30. I think the most important aspect of a pick is that the player using is comfortable with it, and that it fits with your playing style. That being said, this is a pretty versatile overall pick that I could see becoming my preferred choice on electric guitar.

The reason these particular Herdim picks are sought after is actually the dimpled portion on the fat end of the pick. Normally, this would be the part of the pick you hold, and it is a very comfortable grip for extra control and stability. But The Edge used the pick upside down so that the dimples would grip and release the strings momentarily, almost like a pinch. As any guitar player knows, there is a huge tonal difference between fingerstyle and using a pick, and the same principles apply to picking strings with the dimpled portion of a Herdim (versus a regular, smooth pick). It really gives the notes a more aggressive, brighter, and more articulate attack. This becomes critical with The Edge's use of dotted eighth delays, where that initial note may repeat several times in rhythm. While you certainly do not NEED a Herdim pick to play notes like that effectively, I have to admit that there is a noticeable difference in single notes and appreciated sequences. For chord play and faster parts, I still prefer to hold the pick the normal way, as the string can occasionally catch up on the dimples or on any rough surfaces around the top of the pick.

In terms of thickness, I believe the Blue one is the thickest (at 0.88mm), but because it is a nylon pick, I was pleasantly surprised at how it still has a bit of flexibility. My normal picks are the Dunlop Tortex (orange) or Ultex (clear), both at 0.60mm. In terms of rigidity, the Blue 0.88m Herdim is probably between an Orange and Yellow Tortex, despite being thicker than both. Thicker picks transfer energy more efficiently to the string, but can be harder to play rhythmically (particularly for big strums) and have less dynamic range. The Blue Herdim, in addition to having the cool upside-down-dimple-face trick, is a pretty good compromise across all of these different needs.

With all that being said, the Herdims are EXPENSIVE (paid a bit over a dollar a pick in this purchase), and I didn't want 12 of them initially, but that was the only bundle that made sense. My local stores don't carry them, and even a lot of the popular online guitar sites don't seem to have them. I have to think there are more cost-effective alternatives, and I might explore that. Some people even rough up their own picks with a file. Dunlop makes a gray nylon pick with dimples, but the grip parts are higher and less uniform, so it's less predictable as it rakes across a string.

This is probably the most anyone has ever written about a one dollar piece of plastic/nylon, and I am irrationally proud of that. Given all of the above, I think the Herdim picks ARE the best choice for me, and totally lived up to the mythical expectations, but I would also hope that I get some life out of them and do not have to continue ordering them, due to the premium price. Given what people are willing to spend on other types of guitar gear, it does seem like a pretty reasonable premium for what is really an important and underappreciated aspect of good tone.

user_history.review_text:
I’ve previously reviewed the Stellar X2 Vintage and found it to be an excellent sounding mic for a variety of applications.

The Stellar X3 is meant to be an upgrade, and the price reflects that.

Opening the packaging, there’s a decent compact protective case that holds the mic, shock mount and foam shield.

The X2 Vintage had a pretty generic / affordable “clip” style shock mount that did the job. The X3 goes a step further and has a VERY sturdy threaded mount that suspends the mic perfectly within the shock cage. Looks cool, very like a Neumann mount (which cost between $150-300 just for the shock mount). More importantly, it works really well. Just moving the mic stand around during placement, I noticed less noise compared to the X2 Vintage.

The mic itself has a nice heft and feels very solid. Aesthetically it’s been upgraded with a sleek black livery and new TZ badge. I didn’t think the X2 looked cheap by any means but the X3 LOOKS more expensive.

The X3 now includes switches for a -10db pad (for loud sources) and a high pass / proximity filter (minimize excessive bass when you’re up close and also background rumble). Nice to have, convenient to be on the mic and potentially means less to fix in mix.

With this mic, they’re aiming for a more “vintage” tonality, when compared to the regular X2. However, that’s basically what the X2 Vintage was about..

In use, there’s a smooth top end on vocals, no spiky presence, suits my voice well (and that’s what this is about; you find a mic that suits YOUR voice).

For acoustic, my “lawsuit” era Takamine can be a little boomy and typically a mic with more presence would be better BUT I captured some nice recording by close mic-ing and using the proximity filter, which cut out some unpleasant lower frequencies and resonance. Made it easier to EQ.

Compared to the X2 Vintage, the X3 is even smoother and darker, so bear that in mind. It’ll work really well on bright sources to tame them and adds a vintage / polished vibe to everything you try it on. Got some great recordings close up on my amp playing hard rock (and blended with an SM7B it was excellent), and again it was perfect for the rock vocals I was attempting.

On my excessively warm acoustic (with coated strings that I’m starting to regret), I felt it lacked enough presence BUT.. I’ve got some pencil mics with a lot of presence for that. Use the right tool for the job.

In terms of value, I feel like TZ have created an excellent mic that stands out in a pretty competitive price bracket. But if you don’t have X3 money, the X2 Vintage kit is pretty darn close, shock mount aside. Lovely mics.

Almost skipped over this because I have enough power supplies for all my boards but.. this one is a BATTERY!

7 outlets, all 9V but I feel like this is aimed at mini / portable boards that typically have mini pedals, which mostly have a low(er) power draw anyway.

Charged it up within a few hours (used an Apple 10W iPad adapter) and it was good to go. Simple small LED shows charging and battery status. Would be nice to have a better sense of overall charge levels after some use.. basic LED level meter would be nice!

Battery lasts a claimed 8hrs with continuous use, plenty for any gig and for many practice sessions. I forgot to turn it off overnight and it still had a charge the following day and was able to be used for several more hours (since none of the pedals were engaged overnight I guess).

Tested it out with a few gain pedals and was pleased that it doesn’t introduce any additional unwanted noise.

The included cables are cheap and on the shorter side but they work fine and, again, this is aimed at small boards.

Overall it’s really useful and very affordable.

If you want a pedalboard power supply that’ll work literally ANYWHERE, and to not worry about bad outlets at a venue, this is a great idea.

user_history.review_text:
Frustration free packaging is minimalist as usual, no plastics. Nice.

Cables are somewhat thin; thinner than MonoPrice and CableMatters XLR cables. Very flexible though, which can be an advantage!

Doesn’t really give many specifics on the type of cable shielding. For example, CableMatters has multiple shields, insulates the individual wires within the cable, etc. Amazon just mentions an “inner copper spiral shielding”.

The connectors are solidly built, not exactly Neutriks but the locking mechanism feels solid on both and no issues plugging / unplugging. They’ve machined little grooves into the barrels that help with grip when unplugging, which is a nice detail.

The XLR barrels are a little shorter than on some other brands, which is actually very useful in tight spaces. The strain relief plastic is short and squishy, more so than on MonoPrice or CableMatters products. Not sure how effective it is but, again, it doesn’t get in the way and the overall shortness / flexibility can help. For example, the CableMatters XLR barrel rubs against my VIVO mic mount, putting a slight pressure on the SM7B connector. The MonoPrice XLR is even longer and I won’t even try it. The AmazonBasics fits just right!

Pins are brass, silver plated. Both MonoPrice and CableMatters use gold plated pins.

The shielding and pin plating being different or unknown / lesser quality might not be a big deal for 6ft and under. For longer cable lengths, go with a brand that has the best possible shielding to maintain signal integrity, especially when recording.

Testing with a Shure SM7B along with a Cathedral Pipes “Durham” mic booster, which needs +48V phantom power. Audio interface is an "old but gold" Focusrite LS56. Monitoring on Sennheiser HD280 Pros. Hopefully this lets me test every aspect of the cable accurately and fairly.

I used 2 channels on the same interface, one wired with a pretty expensive (and long) Monster XLR cable to a mic booster, then from the booster to mic with a short 3ft CableMatters XLR cable.
The 2nd channel was wired purely with the two AmazonBasics 6ft XLR cables, either side of the mic booster.

Noise floor was pretty indistinguishable between the two setups. Recorded audio quality was also close to the point of being unable to tell them apart.

For the short cable runs, whatever shielding Amazon is using is definitely up to par and I’ll likely permanently swap out the stiffer CableMatters XLR to reduce pressure on the SM7B’s XLR connector (the AmazonBasic’s shorter barrel really makes a difference here).

Great value, great performance. Chuffed.

user_history.review_text:
I’m usually more of an overdrive guy, pushing the amp over the edge or stacking them for more gain / sonic flavors.

But I’ve also got a few distortion pedals that are kinda fun, so was looking forward to testing the GIHUBO GH-23.

Out the box, looks like it means business! Dark design, some kind of wild graphic. Tone, Level and Gain controls. 9V input was a little offset, required some jiggling to get my connector fully seated. Foot switch seems sturdy enough and the pots rotate fairly smoothly.

I clicked it on, expecting some heavy, Mesa Boogie goodness and instead.. got a Metal Zone meme approximation of early 90s scooped mids distortion. Just.. awful.

I’m testing this through the green channel of a 5150 III head. It made it sound the worst it’s ever sounded. No joke. I’ve got over 50 pedals and THIS.. this is probably the one that sounds the worst.

Usually with every pedal I purchase or test for review, there’s at least one sound I can find where the pedal redeems itself, and I’ll noodle along and have a good time. Not this one. I simply can’t get a good sound out of it. There’s no body to the tone.. it’s super harsh in a way that goes beyond “well it might sound good in the mix”. No. It sounds like a bad distortion from an early 90s multifx unit. The tone control goes from “muffled and scooped” to “omg my ears are bleeding” treble overload. Also, you barely hear a shift in gain amount as you rotate the Gain knob. It’s just “on” and maybe gets slightly more saturated.

In my mind, Boogies are super versatile high gain amps. This is definitely high gain but has the most limited tonal palette of any dirt box I’ve ever played through.

GIHUBO is a new brand to me. Based on this distortion pedal alone I would probably steer clear of them BUT.. I also got their OD pedal and it is legitimately great fun to play with.

So avoid THIS pedal for sure, but check out their OD pedal.

[[VIDEOID:712ee0ef42350f3a6b4d0617844d5595]] Uploaded a video briefly demonstrating the impact of each band.

My thoughts about the Vivlex Guitar EQ are overwhelmingly positive.

EQ is a utility, tone shaping pedal. Not necessarily exciting but can fundamentally change or (re)shape how your guitar sounds.

Some iconic boost / overdrive pedals will bump the mids and that’s something this pedal can do quite easily. Amps can respond differently to being overdriven with different frequencies, so there’s lots of room for experimentation.

When switching guitars, you can compensate for different pickup types, and that worked great with the Vivlex when I swapped between a Les Paul and Tele / Strat single coils, really helped beef up the single coils. For the humbuckers, cutting a little of the lower frequencies helps tighten things up, reduce woolliness.

The volume has a decent range. As you bump frequencies, the overall output increases. Being able to offset with a master volume is super handy. But also, this can function as a clean, shaped boost.

My only criticism relates to the amount of noise generated when you use more exaggerated frequency boosts. The easy workaround (demonstrated in my video) is to SUBTRACT frequencies to shape your tone and use the volume control to offset the level decrease. That way, there is very little or no additional noise added.

Build quality is solid. Footswitch feels sturdy, 9V input is aligned correctly and the sliders have center detents for zero, handy.

Value wise, it’s really cheap and works great.

Overall, I’m giving 5 stars because it does everything an EQ pedal should do for under $30.
